extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in an introduction-to-proofs / discrete mathematics course
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standard methods for proving subset relations, set equalities, and for disproving universally quantified or conditional statements (counterexamples). Covers direct/contrapositive/contradiction templates, element-chasing using set definitions, case analysis, algebraic manipulations (divisibility, geometric series), and equality-by-double-inclusion or by chains of equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Prove A ⊆ B (Direct approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ⊆ B, prove the conditional statement “If a ∈ A, then a ∈ B” directly by assuming a ∈ A and deducing a ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof template: Suppose a ∈ A. (Use definitions/facts about A and a.) Deduce a ∈ B. Conclude A ⊆ B. The text recommends the direct approach as usually the most straightforward and uses it in most examples; explicit element-chasing is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Prove A ⊆ B (Contrapositive approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove A ⊆ B by proving the contrapositive: assume a ∉ B and deduce a ∉ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template: Suppose a ∉ B. Deduce a ∉ A. Conclude A ⊆ B. Use when contrapositive reasoning is more expedient than a direct argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove A ⊆ B by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: You may prove A ⊆ B by contradiction: assume (a ∈ A) ∧ (a ∉ B) and deduce a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an alternative template; the book notes it is sometimes used but that direct proof is usually simplest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove A = B by double inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets are equal, show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A; together these imply A = B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template: [Prove A ⊆ B.] [Prove B ⊆ A.] Then conclude A = B. This is presented as the standard procedure for set equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving subset relations via element-chasing using definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the formal definitions of set operations (union, intersection, Cartesian product, power set, divisibility, etc.) to translate membership statements into simpler claims about elements and then deduce desired memberships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: From (a,b) ∈ A×B deduce a ∈ A and b ∈ B; from X ∈ P(A) deduce X ⊆ A; from a ∈ A∩B deduce a ∈ A and a ∈ B. The book repeatedly 'suppose an element of the left-hand set' and then applies definitions to chase membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis for unions and related proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When membership comes from a union or similar disjunction, consider cases (e.g., X ∈ P(A) ∪ P(B) means X ∈ P(A) or X ∈ P(B)) and show the conclusion in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To show P(A)∪P(B) ⊆ P(A∪B), split into Case 1: X⊆A, Case 2: X⊆B; in each case deduce X⊆A∪B. Note: do not duplicate effort when one case covers the intersection of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equalities by a chain of set-theoretic equalities (manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes prove A = B by manipulating one side via known logical/set identities until you obtain the other; show a sequence of equal expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A×(B∩C) = (A×B)∩(A×C) proved by rewriting set-builder conditions, using (P ⇔ P∧P), rearranging conjunctions, and applying definitions. This can shorten proofs when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraic identities and known formulas in set/number proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When sets are defined using number-theoretic expressions, use algebraic formulas (e.g., geometric series) or prime-factorization reasoning to establish divisibility and sum properties needed for the set argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In proving numbers of form 2^{n−1}(2^n−1) are perfect, use the geometric series sum formula ∑_{k=0}^{n−1}2^k = 2^n−1 and factorization/divisor structure to show the sum of proper divisors equals the number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving divisibility-based subset relations via factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: For sets defined by divisibility (e.g., {x : 35|x}), show containment by writing an element as a multiple and factoring to show divisibility by the relevant factors; conversely use prime-factorization arguments to deduce larger divisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 18|a ⇒ 6|a by writing a=18c and factoring; for the converse intersection-to-product inclusion, argue that 5|a and 7|a implies 35|a by prime factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Cartesian product membership to transfer membership information
rubrics_metrics.description: To relate A×C and B×C, use that (a,c) ∈ A×C implies a ∈ A and c ∈ C; when C is nonempty, existence of a c permits embedding single-element arguments to prove A⊆B (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If A×C = B×C and C ≠ ∅, pick c∈C; for any a∈A, (a,c)∈A×C = B×C so (a,c)∈B×C and hence a∈B, showing A⊆B (and symmetrically B⊆A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent/obvious subset facts may be used without full proof (mental check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subset statements (e.g., A∩B ⊆ A, A ⊆ A∪B) are transparent enough that the book uses them without formal proof, though it advises the reader to verify them mentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: You don't need to prove extremely obvious inclusions in exercises unless asked, but you should be able to mentally justify them; if you cannot, spend more time on the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof of universal statements via counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a universally quantified statement ∀x∈S, P(x), produce a single x∈S for which P(x) is false (a counterexample); this proves the negation ∃x∈S,¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template: Find and present an explicit x ∈ S with computation or reasoning showing P(x) fails. Example: show f(11)=121 so the claim “for all n, n^2−n+11 is prime” is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof of conditional statements by exhibiting a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P(x)⇒Q(x), produce an x for which P(x) is true and Q(x) is false (i.e., a witness that violates the implication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is similar to the universal-case counterexample pattern specialized to implications: exhibit x with antecedent true and consequent false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic step: test several examples to build intuition before attempting a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting a proof or disproof, compute several sample cases to detect patterns or counterexamples and guide the choice of proof technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tabulating values of n^2−n+11 for n=... suggested the conjecture might be true until n=11 provided a counterexample. The book recommends gathering such evidence but emphasizes it is not a substitute for proof.
